title: Philadelphia Museum Closure Prompts Funding Offer and Planned City Hearings
summary:
Philadelphia's Academy of Natural Sciences Museum has closed, leaving families without a familiar place to explore dinosaurs, animals and natural history. After a September 1 announcement gave visitors one month's notice, thousands came for final visits before the September 30 closure.

Founded in 1812, the Academy opened to the public in 1828. It became the first institution in the world to display a dinosaur skeleton in 1868. Generations of children have since visited its exhibits, which also included animal dioramas, live animals and changing displays. Dioramas are scenes that show animals in settings resembling their habitats.

Drexel University, which assumed financial responsibility for the Academy in 2011, said costs had risen and attendance had declined after the pandemic. The university has also faced its own financial difficulties. The museum reduced staffing and hours in 2025 and cancelled its 2026 summer camp.

Attendance surged during the final weeks. Revenue was more than 20 times higher than during the previous September. Supporters organized rallies, marches and an online petition with more than 114,000 signatures. Some criticized Drexel for giving little warning and not explaining what keeping the museum open would cost.

Less than a week before closing, the William Penn Foundation offered a year of bridge funding. That means temporary financial support while a longer solution is explored. Drexel said it was exploring the possibility of working with the foundation, but needed a sustainable long-term plan before considering reopening.

The Academy's collection contains more than 19 million specimens, including Thomas Jefferson's fossils and plant samples gathered by Lewis and Clark. It also holds 73,000 holotype specimens: reference samples scientists use to define and name species. Drexel said it would preserve access for students and researchers, although access for the public remains uncertain.

Philadelphia's city council has proposed zoning changes that would make selling the building or converting it to other uses more difficult. It also plans public hearings to investigate the closure and possible solutions. Whether or when the museum will reopen remains uncertain.
why_it_matters: The closure removes a familiar learning destination for families. The funding offer and planned hearings concern whether public visits can resume, while Drexel says students and researchers will retain collection access.
